documents.source_document: Document 5 - President Andrew Jackson, Second Annual Message to Congress, December 6, 1830
documents.source_text: . . . The consequences of a speedy removal will be important to the United States, to individual States, and to the Indians [Native Americans] themselves. The pecuniary [financial] advantages which it promises to the Government are the least of its recommendations. It puts an end to all possible danger of collision between the authorities of the General [Federal] and State Governments on account of the Indians. It will place a dense and civilized population in large tracts of country now occupied by a few savage hunters. By opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites it will incalculably [greatly] strengthen the SW [southwestern] frontier and render the adjacent States strong enough to repel future invasions without remote aid. It will relieve the whole State of Mississippi and the western part of Alabama of Indian occupancy, and enable those States to advance rapidly in population, wealth, and power. It will separate the Indians from immediate contact with settlements of whites; free them from the power of the States. . . .

documents.source_document: Document 6 - General Council of the Cherokee Nation, address to the people of the United States, New Echota, July 17, 1830
documents.source_text:
. . . We are not willing to remove; and if we could be brought to this extremity [last step], it would be not by argument, not because our judgment was satisfied, not because our condition will be improved; but only because we cannot endure to be deprived of our national and individual rights and subjected to a process of intolerable oppression.
We wish to remain on the land of our fathers. We have a perfect and original right to claim without interruption or molestation [being bothered]. The treaties with us, and laws of the United States made in pursuance of treaties, guaranty our residence, and our privileges and secure us against intruders. Our only request is that these treaties may be fulfilled, and these laws executed. . . .
documents._pointer: Cherokee Phoenix, July 24, 1830. Text follows TAH ('Address to the People of the United States, by the General Council of the Cherokee Nation') and WCU Hunter Library transcription no. 14 ('claim', 'residence, and'), which agree; WCU no. 99 reads 'remain' and 'residence and', and carries the dateline 'New Echota, C. N. July 17' (its '1930' is a typo). Two records to one (D-U1); page scan not checked. Dateline: TAH gives only 'July 1830' and the Phoenix prints no dateline; 'New Echota, C.N. · July 17, 1830' is printed after the signatures in the 1830 pamphlet Removal of the Cherokee Indians, Digital Library of Georgia, dlg_zlna_pam008 (https://dlg.usg.edu/record/dlg_zlna_pam008). Bracketed glosses ours. BEFORE WE TALK.

prompt: Name the principle both documents are really arguing about -- then say how each side uses it.
intro: No hints, no starter, no checklist. This is the one you do the way you would on the exam.
model_response: Both documents argue over Federalism and Natural Rights at once. Document 5 treats removal as a matter for the state and federal governments to settle between themselves. Document 6 answers that the Cherokee's “original right” to their land came before any government's say over it -- the same disagreement that a few years later Marshall would rule on in Document 7, in the Cherokee's favor.
